entity.name: Umar
entity.description: The caliph who conquered two empires in a decade. Umar ibn al-Khattab transformed from a fierce opponent of Islam into its most powerful early ruler, expanding the caliphate across Persia and two-thirds of the Byzantine Empire. He introduced the Islamic Hijri calendar and was assassinated by a Persian slave in 644.

story.name: Umar ibn al-Khattab
story.description: From sworn enemy of Muhammad to Islam's most powerful caliph. Conversion at swordpoint, conquest of Persia in two years, opening Jerusalem to Jewish worship, and assassination by a Persian slave.

moments.name: Umar Converts to Islam After Setting Out to Kill Muhammad
moments.subtitle: The man who drew his sword to murder the Prophet sheathes it and kneels instead
moments.description: In 616, Umar ibn al-Khattab set out with a sword to kill Muhammad, whom he saw as a threat to Quraysh unity. On the way, a friend told him his own sister had secretly converted. Umar stormed to her house and found her reciting the Quran. After a violent confrontation that left his sister bleeding, Umar demanded to read the verses himself. Moved by the words of Surat Ta-Ha, the fearsome wrestler broke down in tears and declared his faith. He then marched to Muhammad with the same sword and converted in front of the gathered Muslims. Umar's conversion was so pivotal that Muslims began openly praying at the Kaaba for the first time.

moments.name: Umar Brokers Abu Bakr's Election as First Caliph at Saqifah
moments.subtitle: A political masterstroke on the day of Muhammad's funeral prevents the young faith from splitting apart
moments.description: On 8 June 632, the day Muhammad died, Medina's native Ansar faction held a secret meeting at Saqifah Bani Saadah to choose their own leader, excluding the Meccan Muhajireen emigrants. Umar ibn al-Khattab discovered the meeting and rushed there with Abu Bakr and Abu Ubaidah ibn al-Jarrah. Facing a unified bloc of Ansar tribes, Umar divided them by exploiting the old rivalry between the Aws and Khazraj clans, then publicly pledged allegiance to Abu Bakr as a unity candidate. The gathering followed suit. This improvised political intervention established the caliphate as an institution and set the precedent for Islamic political succession.

moments.name: Umar Fights in the Battle of Badr, Islam's First Major Victory
moments.subtitle: 313 Muslims defeat an army of 1,000 Quraysh in a battle that transforms a persecuted sect into a military power
moments.description: In March 624, at the wells of Badr southwest of Medina, a force of roughly 313 Muslims led by Muhammad faced a Quraysh army of about 1,000 soldiers. Umar ibn al-Khattab fought as one of Muhammad's key companions in this first major pitched battle between the early Muslim community and the Meccan establishment. Against heavy odds, the Muslim force won a decisive victory, killing roughly 70 Quraysh fighters and capturing another 70. The Battle of Badr established the Muslim community as a serious military and political force in Arabia, and later Islamic tradition treats it as a divinely ordained turning point.

moments.name: Umar Lifts the Ban on Jews Entering Jerusalem
moments.subtitle: The conqueror reverses centuries of exclusion and lets Jews worship in their holiest city again
moments.description: In 637, Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab accepted the surrender of Jerusalem from the Byzantine Patriarch Sophronius. According to Jewish tradition, Umar reversed the longstanding Christian ban on Jews entering the city and permitted them to worship there once again. The caliph reportedly visited the Temple Mount, which had been used as a rubbish dump under Byzantine rule, and ordered it cleaned. Umar's conquest of Jerusalem brought the city under Muslim control for the first time and established a policy of relative religious tolerance that allowed Jews, Christians, and Muslims to coexist in the holy city.

moments.name: A Persian Slave Stabs Caliph Umar During Morning Prayers
moments.subtitle: The ruler of the largest empire on Earth is killed by a man he had conquered
moments.description: In November 644, Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab was leading the dawn prayer at Al-Masjid an-Nabawi in Medina when Abu Lu'lu'a Firuz, a Persian Christian slave, attacked him with a double-bladed dagger, stabbing him six times. Firuz, who had been captured during the Islamic conquest of Persia, reportedly held a personal grievance over taxes imposed by his master. Umar died from his wounds three days later at age 59 or 60. Before dying, he appointed a six-member council to choose his successor, which eventually selected Uthman ibn Affan. Umar was buried beside Muhammad and Abu Bakr in what is now the Prophet's Mosque.
